headline: Profit slumps on one-time charges as revenue holds steady
summary_short: Revenue was roughly flat at $34,253M (-0.7% y/y), but net income fell 23.3% y/y to $3,835M and diluted EPS dropped to $0.92 from $1.18, weighed down by a $746M held-for-sale loss on Verizon's international wireline unit, $397M of severance charges, and higher SG&A.
summary_long: Revenue was essentially flat at $34,253M (-0.7% y/y), as a Consumer-segment decline was mostly offset by Business-segment growth. Operating income fell 12.2% y/y to $7,179M and net income fell 23.3% y/y to $3,835M ($0.92 diluted EPS, down from $1.18), driven by a $746M net loss on classifying Verizon's international wireline business as held-for-sale, $397M of workforce-reduction severance charges, $200M of asset-rationalization charges, and $135M of Frontier acquisition/integration costs, plus a higher 25.1% effective tax rate. Cash fell to $1,752M as Verizon repaid roughly $12.4B of Frontier-related debt. Verizon raised its full-year 2026 share-repurchase target from $3.0B to up to $4.5B; capex guidance stands at $16.0-16.5B.

drivers.explanation: Consumer segment revenue declined 1.5% while Business segment revenue grew 2.6%; the net consolidated effect was a slight y/y decrease.

The filing attributes changes in operating income to the same revenue and expense factors discussed above, chiefly the SG&A special items (held-for-sale loss, severance, asset rationalization, Frontier integration costs).
Tracks the same operating-income dynamics: roughly flat revenue against SG&A special items and higher depreciation from Frontier-related assets.
Per the filing, EBITDA changes were primarily a result of the same consolidated revenue and operating-expense factors described for operating income.
Reflects the lower operating income plus higher interest expense from higher average debt balances, and lower other income from fair-value adjustments on investments and derivatives.
Lower pretax income combined with a higher 25.1% effective tax rate (vs 22.5% a year ago), driven by a nondeductible loss on the international wireline held-for-sale classification.
Tracks the net-income decline; diluted share count fell only slightly (4,171M vs 4,228M) on buybacks, so nearly all of the EPS drop reflects lower earnings.
Cost of wireless equipment fell $1.1B on lower device-upgrade volumes tied to a strategic pullback in upgrades, more than offsetting the slight revenue decline.

Cash fell as financing outflows -- roughly $12.4B of Frontier-related debt repayment, $9.5B of acquisition spending, dividends, and buybacks -- exceeded operating cash flow and new borrowing proceeds.
The current portion of long-term debt fell as Verizon repaid roughly $12.4 billion of principal debt assumed in the Frontier acquisition during the first half of 2026.
Retained earnings grew as net income exceeded dividends declared, modestly outweighing the increase in treasury stock from buybacks.
Share count fell as Verizon repurchased 72.0 million shares for $3.5 billion via accelerated share-repurchase agreements during the first half of 2026.

Results were weighed down by one-time items -- a held-for-sale loss on the international wireline unit, workforce-reduction severance, and Frontier integration costs -- while the company raised its 2026 buyback target and kept capex guidance intact.
